• Other names: Indian toothcup, Ammannia 'Bonsai', Rotala 'Bonsai'
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: medium
  • Substrate: any (preferably nutrient-rich)
  • Can float: yes
  • Growth form: stem
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Placement: midground or background
  • Height: up to 10–20 cm
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: head cuttings

Rotala indica is native to India and Southeast Asia, where it grows along rice paddies, marshes and low-lying fields as an annual weed. This amphibious plant is also an introduced species and a weed in rice-growing regions in Congo, Italy, Portugal and Spain, and in California and Louisiana in the United States.
Rotala indica suits both nano and large aquariums. The author recommends a tank of no less than 40 litres.

Rotala indica is an ideal species for beginners, with low to moderate care demands. Under optimal conditions it grows very fast and can even become a problem, so prune regularly, removing overgrown stems and dead leaves with tweezers, and remove all clippings from the tank. You can also gently stir or brush the dense stems to bring debris to the surface and sieve it out.

Regular additions of chelated iron, phosphorus and potassium give lush reddish-pink colour and prevent stunting. Change a quarter of the water weekly with dechlorinated water, provide enough light and keep nitrates around 5 ppm to encourage reddish shoots.

Some aquascapers make bonsai trees by attaching the plant to driftwood and trimming it constantly; after trimming it branches from every leaf node and becomes very bushy.

Planting and propagation

  • Remove the plant from the pot.
  • Separate the stems from the rock wool, disinfect and rinse them thoroughly.
  • Do not plant in a bunch; leave at least 3–5 cm between stems to prevent overcrowding.

You can also leave it floating until it grows roots, but it then needs a lot of nutrients in the water column.

Propagation is by stem cuttings: cut the upper part of the stem with sharp scissors just above a leaf node, ideally 10 cm long. Make a hole 3–4 cm deep in the substrate, place the stem in it and cover. Healthy stems will root and grow into new plants.

Problems

  • Chlorosis: pale, yellow or yellow-white leaves caused by insufficient chlorophyll. Main causes are lack of iron, nitrogen deficiency and a very acidic or alkaline pH. Dose chelated iron and keep nitrates and pH ideal.
  • Stunted growth: caused by insufficient trace elements, low nitrates or inadequate CO2. Correct these, raise the light intensity and test the water regularly.
  • Loss of leaves: indicates too little light, or the lower part is shaded by overly dense growth. Under low light it often has only 2 leaves per internode, under medium to high light 3–4. Increase light and thin or trim dense growth.
  • Holes in the lower leaves: the cause is hard to pinpoint; start by checking light and minerals.

This plant adapts to a wide range of water values.

Temperature: the optimal range is 20–28 °C, so it thrives in most tropical aquariums provided temperature fluctuations are small.

pH: 6.0–7.5. Test the water regularly with an accurate test kit.

Hardness: it tolerates soft to fairly hard water; keep it at 2–12 °dGH.

Lighting: medium light, about 30–50 PAR from full-spectrum bulbs. The leaves are naturally green but turn reddish-pink under sufficiently bright light. Under low light the plant grows thin and the shoots become yellow-green.

Substrate: it can be planted or grown floating, as it takes up nutrients from both the substrate and the water column, but once planted it grows faster and more stably. A nutrient-rich substrate is recommended, for example ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Carib Sea Eco-Complete or Seachem Fluorite. These fine-grained substrates keep the plant firmly rooted and help maintain its bunchy appearance. Provide a substrate bed at least 5 cm deep. In sand or gravel it is also possible, but root tabs and/or liquid fertilizers are needed.

CO2 and nutrients: with a nutrient-rich substrate and some nitrates and phosphates in the water, it thrives without supplementation, though regular fertilizing keeps it healthy. CO2 is not essential once the plant has adjusted, but it promotes rapid growth, density and vivid colour.

Important: if you keep shrimp with it, note that high CO2 levels and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Rotala indica is a flowering plant in the loosestrife family Lythraceae and the genus Rotala, which comprises fast-growing stem plants. It has erect, delicate stems (on average 10–20 cm tall) with thin, rounded or obovate, obtuse leaves about 1.5–2 cm long. The leaves are usually lush green, but may develop pink or red hues at the shoot tips under high light. Leaves are arranged oppositely in perpendicular pairs, and flowers occur singly in the leaf axils or in short, dense spikes. It can be grown emersed or submersed, like its close relative Rotala rotundifolia.

Difference between Rotala indica and Rotala rotundifolia

The two species are often mistaken for each other, especially when grown emersed with round leaves. Underwater, Rotala indica can be told apart by its slightly smaller size, more rounded leaves, and solitary or spike inflorescence as opposed to terminal inflorescence.

Rotala indicaRotala rotundifolia
SizeSmaller (up to 20+ cm)Bigger (up to 30+ cm)
Leaf shapeMore roundedMore narrow and lanceolate
Leaf structureThicker at the tipsThin
InflorescenceSolitary or spikeTerminal

Benefits

  • Aquascape: one of the best choices for jungle aquascapes.
  • Foraging place: its leaves create a lot of surface for biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and baby shrimp.
  • Shelter: provides hiding spots for shy fish and shrimp.
  • Removal of excess nutrients: it takes up nitrates, ammonia and phosphates from the water.
  • Oxygenation: helps oxygenate the water column.
  • Reduces algae: it is so greedy for nutrients that it outcompetes algae. Algae-eating species such as Amano shrimp, Nerite snails and Otocinclus catfish can help further.

Compatible tankmates

  • Fish: bettas, swordtails, tetras, pearl gourami, honey gourami, harlequin rasbora, zebra danio, cherry barbs, platies, guppies, Endlers, mollies, Otocinclus, pygmy corydoras, etc.
  • Dwarf shrimp: Neocaridina (red cherry, blue velvet, snowball, black rose, orange sakura, green jade, rili) or Caridina (crystal red, Caridina cf. babaulti, blue tiger), as well as Amano, ghost, bamboo and vampire shrimp.
  • Freshwater snails: Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails, etc.

Avoid keeping it with crayfish or freshwater crabs, which will tear up the foliage and uproot the plant, and with aggressive fish known to eat plants, such as Texas cichlids, Jack Dempsey, red devil and oscars.

Buying and quarantine

It can be obtained from online vendors, local fish stores and nurseries. Choose plants with a lush appearance, vibrant green or reddish colour, healthy stems and roots, and fresh leaves without discoloration, holes or rips. Two pots or bunches of about five stems are enough to aquascape a small tank.

Unless the plant was grown in vitro in an undamaged, unopened pot, quarantine and disinfect it. It can carry parasites, hitchhikers such as pest snails, or predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs), and may have been treated with pesticides that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Conclusion

It combines well with other easy plants such as Anacharis, Anubias nana, Java fern and water wisteria, or close relatives such as Rotala rotundifolia and Rotala macandra.
